output.title: Why the route is the product
output.content:
Batching a groomer's day by neighbourhood saves about an hour of driving; that hour is the whole pitch.

When Delia first booked customers in the order they called, her van crossed Port Alder four times a day. Tidewell now sorts the day into clusters, and three small rules add up to the hour:

Stops in the same neighbourhood are offered together.

The first slot of the day is the one closest to the van's home.

A cancellation pulls a nearby booking forward instead of leaving a gap.

The route is the product. The booking form is just how it gets fed.

output.title: Raising the price without losing anyone
output.content:
Raising $29 to $39 with grandfathering lost nobody; the new price only ever applied to people who never saw the old one.

On 1 August the monthly price went from $29 to $39. Every groomer who was already paying kept $29 for as long as they stay. New signups see only $39, so nobody is ever told that they are paying more than someone else.

The email I sent to the forty existing groomers was four sentences long, and two of them replied with a thank-you.

output.title: Routes & ramps: <van> life 🚐
output.content:
A day in a grooming van is mostly ramps, parking and low bridges, and the software only sees the addresses.

Ramp angles decide which dogs can be booked into which van.

Low bridges decide which streets the route optimiser may use.

Parking decides whether the next stop starts on time.

output.title: How Tidewell started
output.content:
Tidewell started in January 2026 with a spreadsheet and a phone call to Delia, who ran a one-van grooming shop in Port Alder and kept her bookings on a paper calendar.

By March she was the first paying customer, and the spreadsheet had become a booking form with a route on the back of it.
